title: gpu-autoscaler-investigation-scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for the recent dedicated GPU pool capacity thrash incidents (late Feb -> early Mar 2026). Mostly breadcrumbs: commands I ran, raw snippets, naive hypotheses, short experiment notes. This is a working note — not polished.

High-level symptom summary (observed):
- Production route A experienced intermittent 503/latency spikes during scale-down windows (predominantly midnight UTC) between 2026-02-26 and 2026-03-05.
- Autoscaler frequently removed recently-created GPU nodes while they were still finishing model binary caching / container warm-up. Subsequent cold requests queued and caused a short but sharp spike in request latency which in turn triggered rapid scale-up, creating oscillation (thrash).
- Warm-up time (time between node readiness and first successful stable token-per-second) measured ~22–47s depending on model and image pull.

Commands / queries I ran (with copy-paste-able snippets):
- List pool nodes and age:
  kubectl get nodes -l pool=dedicated-gpu-A -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,AGE:.metadata.creationTimestamp,GPU:.status.allocatable.nvidia\\.com/gpu

- Pod startup timeline (for suspicious pod):
  kubectl -n serving describe pod model-server-6b-xyz | sed -n '1,200p'
  (look for Events: Pulling, Pulled, Created, Started)

- Check kubelet eviction / OOM events:
  journalctl -u kubelet --since "2026-03-02" | grep -i evict -n || true

- HPA / VM autoscaler metrics (Prometheus):
  # ramp = number of pending requests per GPU
  rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{route="/v1/generate",env="prod"}[1m])

- Query for GPU init time (derived metric):
  max_over_time(node_gpu_init_seconds[5m]) by (node)

Raw error snippets observed (copied from logs):
- "2026-03-01T03:14:40Z model-server-6b-xyz ERROR 503 BackendUnavailable: no ready replica (recently terminated)"
- "kubelet[...]: NodeNotReady: image pull timed out for 22s"
- Scheduler message: "insufficient resources: nvidia.com/gpu" (surprising because we had nodes — likely timing race)

Phone-it-in reproduction steps (small test harness run locally / cluster):
1) Create spike: simulate 200 concurrent short chat/generate requests to route-A.
2) Wait for autoscaler to scale out to +8 nodes.
3) Let traffic drop to baseline (2 concurrent) -> autoscaler scales down aggressively with cooldown 60s.
4) Immediately replay 50 concurrent requests at T+30s to provoke warmup vs scale-down race.

Observed: when replay hits during scale-down, new pods land on nodes that were just created (node age 20–45s). Those pods report "model loaded" event only after ~30s; meanwhile front-end sees queued requests and HPA signals further scale-up -> thrash.

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Autoscaler cooldown and scale-down policies too aggressive relative to observed GPU init/warmup time distribution. (Most likely.)
- H2: Node lifecycle hook ordering — node marked "ready" before NV driver and docker image cache fully prepared, so scheduler places pods onto nodes that are not truly ready to serve inference.
- H3: Controller that tracks model cache warm-up does not expose a readiness probe; readiness only depends on container health, not model artifacts being loaded into memory/GPU.
- H4: Network/storage (registry) latency spikes increase image pull time leading to variable startup tail.
- H5: Demand signal for autoscaler uses request rate only; should use queue depth / latency as additional input.

Quick notes on metrics distributions (what I measured):
- 75th percentile GPU init time ~ 28s, 95th ~ 46s (over 72h window) for model family x-large.
- Image pull accounted for ~12–30s when image not cached on node.
- Model binary load (into GPU memory) ~8–22s depending on quantization and sharded load.

Experiments attempted (and outcomes):
Experiment A — increase node scale-down cooldown to 300s for pool-A (test flag):
- Action: updated autoscaler config (field: scaleDownCooldownSeconds = 300).
- Result: oscillation frequency dropped, but average cost up ~5%. Latency spikes reduced but not eliminated (edge cases persisted when image pull happened).

Experiment B — introduce readiness probe that checks "model cache ready" via HTTP /internal/cache/status endpoint:
- Implemented lightweight probe in model-server (PR linked). Hooked into k8s readinessProbe.path = /internal/cache/status returning 200 only when model loaded.
- Result: pods stayed unready longer (as expected). Scheduler delayed placing traffic; latency spikes near eliminated for traffic replay experiments. However, node autoscaler still counted node as ready earlier -> pods scheduled earlier but kept NotReady, which prevented LB from sending traffic. This largely worked but required coordinating readiness + node lifecycle.

Experiment C — pre-warm pool (small static buffer of 1–2 nodes):
- Temporarily pinned minPoolSize=2.
- Result: best UX (no spikes) but cost increased; still want dynamic solution.

Edge cases / weird logs to follow up on:
- Some nodes show kube-proxy flapping and kubelet restarting right after creation -> increases warm time. Need to correlate with cloud-init / kernel module loading (NVIDIA).
- Found one occurrence of NVIDIA driver failing to bind: "nvidia-fabricmanager failed to start" at 2026-03-03T22:11:05Z.

Short-term mitigation proposals (fast):
- Set scaleDownCooldownSeconds = max(3 * p95_gpu_init, 180s) for pools serving latency-sensitive routes.
- Add readiness probe for "model loaded" (already in PR), and gate LB on k8s readiness (we already do). Ensure readiness doesn't become a single-point regression.
- Add an ephemeral warm-start buffer: minNodes = ceil(0.05 * peakCapacity) or absolute 2 nodes for small pools.

Medium-term / more robust fixes:
- Improve autoscaler input signals: feed in queue_depth and 95th latency to prevent scaling down when short bursts are possible.
- Expose node GPU init metrics from cloud-init to controlplane. Autoscaler should treat node as fully available only after node_gpu_init_seconds < threshold. (Change semantics: ready -> available_for_scheduling).
- Implement lazy image caching: keep a light stub image pre-cached and perform lightning-fast hot-patch to pull heavy model only when needed — not sure feasible for large weights.
- Add a "graceful-handoff" where replicas can be scheduled onto nodes but node weight counts as partially available until cache warmed (so scale-down considers this).

Immediate TODOs (my follow-ups):
- [ ] Finish PR for readiness probe and include a feature flag (A/B by pool) — tracked in PR#8912. Owner: Asha.
- [ ] Add a Prom rule for node_gpu_init_seconds and alert if p95 > 40s. Owner: Diego.
- [ ] Update autoscaler config for pool-A to cooldown=300s for next 72h (monitor). Owner: Marta.
- [ ] Correlate kubelet restarts with cloud-init logs on nodes 10.4.*.* (Noah).

Notes for on-call (short playbook):
- If route latency spikes and we see rapid scale-up then scale-down loops: check pool's scaleDownCooldownSeconds and consider raising temporarily.
- Check /internal/cache/status probe responses on model pods. If they report not-ready, check image pull logs: kubectl -n serving logs <pod> -c init-container (if present).
- Search Prometheus for node_gpu_init_seconds and image_pull_seconds series for correlating spikes.

Random misc breadcrumbs (for later):
- Slack thread: #prod-gpu-autoscale on 2026-03-02 03:46 had a pointer to a suspected registry slowdown (us-west2-registry-IOPS).
- JIRA INC-2345 created for the client-impacting incident on 2026-03-01.
- Consider the idea of a "grace period" label on newly created nodes: annotate nodes with cluster.k8s.io/initializing=true and have scheduler treat them as low-weight until annotation removed by a small agent that performs NV driver checks + test inference.

Closing notes (personal):
- Implementing readiness probe gave biggest win for correctness; autoscaler config changes bought time. Need to be careful with increasing minNodes (cost) vs complexity of adding new signals.
- Next step: ship readiness probe behind a flag to pool-A, update autoscaler cooldown, and run 7-day canary while monitoring p95 latency and autoscaler oscillation count.

-- Asha
(edited 2026-03-12)
